title: Massage for a Hangover: Does It Help, and Is It Safe?
excerpt: Can a massage help a hangover? What massage can and can't do the morning after, which types to book or skip, self-massage and the P6 point for nausea, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does massage help a hangover? What it can and can't do, the best and worst types to book, self-massage tips, the P6 point for nausea, and safety tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a massage won't cure a hangover, speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, or "flush toxins" out of your muscles. What it can do is ease some of the parts of a hangover that live in your body rather than your bloodstream: a tight neck and shoulders, a tension-type headache, achy muscles from dancing or sleeping badly, and the general jittery, stressed feeling the morning after. Gentle massage (from a therapist, a partner, or your own hands) is a reasonable comfort measure. Deep tissue work, hot stones, and lying face-down for an hour while dehydrated and queasy are where it tends to go wrong.

**The quick rules:** Rehydrate and eat before any massage. Choose a lighter style (Swedish or a gentle relaxation massage) over deep tissue. Ask to lie on your side or back if you feel sick face-down. Skip saunas and hot stone add-ons. Get up slowly afterward. And if you're still drunk, don't book one at all; most licensed therapists will turn you away, and for good reason.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and practical guidance for social drinkers. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor or get urgent care if** you can't keep fluids down for more than a few hours, you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have a sudden severe headache or the "worst headache of your life," your muscles are severely painful or swollen and your urine is dark brown, you faint or feel faint when you stand, or you notice confusion, chest pain, or shaking and sweating that gets worse as the day goes on rather than better. In an emergency, call 911.

## Does Massage Help a Hangover? What It Can and Can't Do

A hangover is a bundle of overlapping problems, and it helps to separate them before deciding whether a massage is worth your time or money. Researchers who study hangovers generally point to a mix of causes: mild dehydration, poor-quality sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, low-grade inflammation, small swings in blood sugar, and the effects of acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product your liver makes while breaking alcohol down. Congeners (extra chemicals in darker drinks like whiskey and red wine) seem to make things worse for some people.

Massage doesn't touch most of that list. It doesn't change how quickly your liver processes alcohol or acetaldehyde, it doesn't replace lost fluid, and it doesn't settle an irritated stomach. There is no good evidence that massage shortens a hangover overall, and as far as we know, no clinical trial has tested massage as a hangover treatment directly.

What massage *can* plausibly help with are the secondary, body-based symptoms:

- **Neck and shoulder tension.** Sleeping on a friend's couch, in an odd position, or in a deep alcohol-heavy sleep where you don't shift around normally can leave you stiff. Massage is well suited to that.
- **Tension-type headache.** Many hangover headaches have a tension component, the band-like squeeze around the forehead, temples, or back of the head. Some small studies suggest massage can reduce tension-type headache pain, though the research is limited in size and quality.
- **Muscle aches.** A night of dancing, standing in heels, or carrying gear around a festival leaves real muscle soreness. Massage tends to feel good on sore muscles, even if the research on whether it speeds recovery is mixed.
- **Stress and that wired-but-tired feeling.** Hangovers often come with anxiety and restlessness. A calm, quiet massage can help you relax, and some people find it easier to nap afterward.

So the realistic expectation is "I'll feel somewhat more comfortable for a few hours," not "my hangover is gone." If your main problems are nausea and a pounding head, rest, fluids, food, and time will do more. Our guide to [why your body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking) explains the muscle side of things in more detail.

## Why a Hangover Makes Your Body Hurt in the First Place

Understanding where the aches come from makes it clearer why massage helps some symptoms and not others.

**Dehydration and electrolytes.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more than you drink. Mild dehydration can contribute to headache, fatigue, and muscle cramps. Massage won't fix that; water and electrolytes will.

**Inflammation.** Studies of people with hangovers have found raised levels of inflammatory messengers in the blood. Inflammation is one reason you can feel achy and flu-like. Massage hasn't been shown to change this in hangovers.

**Poor sleep and odd sleeping positions.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep later in the night and cuts into REM sleep. Combine that with a strange bed or passing out on your arm, and you wake up stiff and sore. This is the type of ache massage is best at.

**Physical activity you didn't notice.** Alcohol dulls pain signals, so you may dance for three hours, stand all night, or bang into things without registering it until the next day.

**Muscle tension from stress.** Hangover anxiety is real. When you feel on edge, you tend to clench your jaw, hunch your shoulders, and tighten your neck, which feeds tension headaches.

## Can You Get a Massage While Hungover?

Yes, in most cases you can get a massage while hungover, as long as you're sober, reasonably hydrated, and not actively sick. That's an important distinction. Being *hungover* (alcohol has mostly or completely cleared, you just feel rough) is different from being *still drunk* (alcohol is still in your blood, which can easily be the case the morning after a very heavy night).

Most licensed massage therapists won't work on clients who appear intoxicated. Alcohol affects your judgment and your ability to give clear feedback about pressure and pain, it widens blood vessels and can make you more prone to dizziness, and it raises the odds of nausea on the table. If you're unsure whether you've sobered up, our guide to [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) explains why sleep alone doesn't reset your blood alcohol, and why heavy drinkers can still be over the limit at breakfast.

If you're sober but hungover, a few practical points make the appointment much better:

- **Tell your therapist.** You don't need to go into detail. "I'm a bit dehydrated and queasy today, so I'd like lighter pressure and maybe to start on my side" is enough. Therapists hear this all the time, especially at hotels and resorts.
- **Drink water and eat beforehand.** A small, plain meal and a glass or two of water (or an electrolyte drink) an hour before cuts the risk of feeling faint or sick.
- **Use the bathroom first.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and lying still for an hour with a full bladder is miserable.
- **Pick a shorter session.** Thirty to sixty minutes is usually plenty. A ninety-minute deep tissue session is a lot to ask of a dehydrated body.
- **Speak up during the massage.** If you feel nauseous, dizzy, too hot, or the pressure is too much, say so. A good therapist will adjust right away.

## Which Type of Massage Is Best for a Hangover?

Not all massage styles suit a hangover equally. Here's a practical guide.

**Swedish or relaxation massage (best choice for most people).** Long, flowing strokes with light to medium pressure. It's calming and unlikely to make you feel worse. If you only book one thing, book this.

**Head, neck, and shoulder massage.** Many spas offer a short "tension relief" session focusing on the upper back, neck, scalp, and face. These are a good fit for a hangover headache, and you're often seated or lying on your back, which is easier if you're queasy.

**Scalp massage.** Gentle circles over the scalp, temples, and the base of the skull can feel very soothing for a tension-type headache. It's also easy to do yourself (see below).

**Foot massage or reflexology.** A foot massage is relaxing and you can usually sit upright, which suits people who feel sick lying down. Reflexology claims that points on the feet map to organs like the liver. There's no good evidence for that mapping, so think of it simply as a pleasant foot massage rather than a liver treatment.

**Deep tissue massage (usually skip it).** Deep, firm pressure can leave muscles feeling sore for a day or two, and it's uncomfortable when you're already achy and low on fluids. If deep tissue is your usual preference, save it for a day when you feel well.

**Hot stone massage (skip it).** Heat dilates blood vessels and can make dizziness and dehydration worse. Lying on warm stones when your stomach is unsettled isn't pleasant either.

**Thai massage or sports massage (use caution).** These involve stretching, compression, and sometimes a lot of movement. They can be fine if you feel only mildly hungover, but they're more demanding than a relaxation massage.

**Lymphatic drainage massage.** This is a very light technique sometimes marketed for "detox" or hangover puffiness. It's gentle and unlikely to hurt, but there's no good evidence it removes alcohol or toxins. Any de-puffing effect on your face is modest and short-lived, and drinking water and time do most of that work. Our article on [why your face looks puffy after drinking](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) covers what actually helps.

## The Myth That Massage "Flushes Toxins"

You'll often hear that a massage "releases toxins" from your muscles and that you need to drink lots of water afterward to "flush them out." This idea is very common, including in spas, but it isn't supported by evidence.

Alcohol is processed almost entirely by your liver, with a small amount leaving through breath, sweat, and urine. Your liver works at a fairly steady rate (roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults, though it varies with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors). Rubbing your muscles doesn't send alcohol or acetaldehyde anywhere faster, and muscles aren't storing up hangover toxins that a therapist can push out.

The idea that massage clears out lactic acid from muscles has also been questioned by researchers. Lactate is cleared by the body on its own fairly quickly after exercise, and it isn't the main cause of next-day soreness.

The advice to drink water after a massage is still sensible on a hangover day, just for a different reason: you're likely a bit dehydrated already. For the best ways to replace fluid, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## What Can Go Wrong: Risks of a Massage When Hungover

Massage is generally low-risk for healthy people, but a hangover changes the picture a little.

**Feeling faint or dizzy.** Dehydration can lower your blood pressure, and lying still and relaxed for an hour can lower it further. The riskiest moment is when you sit up and stand at the end. Roll onto your side, sit for a minute, then stand slowly. If you feel lightheaded, sit back down.

**Nausea when face-down.** Lying on your stomach with your face in a cradle can make nausea worse, and pressure on your back and belly doesn't help. Starting on your back or side is a simple fix. Some people prefer a seated chair massage on a queasy day.

**Overheating.** Warm rooms, heated tables, heavy blankets, and hot towels can make you feel worse when you're dehydrated. Ask for the heat to be turned down.

**Extra soreness.** Deep pressure on already achy muscles can leave you feeling more beaten up the next day.

**Bruising.** If you take blood thinners, bruise easily, or have taken aspirin or other anti-inflammatory painkillers, firm pressure is more likely to cause bruising. Tell your therapist about any medicines you take.

**Masking something more serious.** Rarely, very heavy drinking can lead to a breakdown of muscle tissue called rhabdomyolysis, especially after a long period lying in one position or after intense exercise. Signs include severe muscle pain, swelling, weakness, and dark brown or tea-colored urine. This needs medical care, not a massage.

## Self-Massage for a Hangover: Simple Techniques You Can Do at Home

You don't need to book anything. Self-massage costs nothing, you can stop the second it feels wrong, and you can do it lying in bed. Here are a few techniques that people commonly find helpful. Use gentle to moderate pressure, breathe slowly, and stop if anything makes your headache sharper.

**1. Temple circles.** Place your fingertips on your temples, just behind the outer corners of your eyes. Make slow, small circles for 30 to 60 seconds. Gentle is better here; the temples are sensitive.

**2. Base of the skull.** Lie on your back or sit with your elbows on a table. Place your fingertips in the soft hollows on either side of your spine where your neck meets your skull. Press gently upward and hold for 20 to 30 seconds, then make small circles. Many tension headaches feel like they start here.

**3. Scalp kneading.** Spread your fingers through your hair and move the scalp in small circles, as if washing your hair slowly. Work from the forehead back to the crown and down to the neck.

**4. Neck and upper shoulders.** Reach across with your right hand to the top of your left shoulder, where the large trapezius muscle sits. Squeeze gently, release, and work along the muscle toward the neck. Switch sides. Rolling your shoulders slowly afterward helps.

**5. Jaw release.** If you clench your teeth during sleep (common after drinking), place your fingertips on the muscle just in front of your ears, below the cheekbones. Open your mouth slightly and make slow circles.

**6. Brow and bridge of the nose.** Gently pinch along your eyebrows from the inner end outward, then press lightly on either side of the bridge of your nose. Some people find this eases a sinus-like pressure headache.

**7. Tennis ball or massage ball.** Lie on your back with a tennis ball under one side of your upper back, between your shoulder blade and spine. Shift your weight slowly to roll the ball around. This is a gentle way to work tight upper-back muscles without much effort.

A cool, damp cloth on your forehead or the back of your neck during or after self-massage can add to the relief. If your headache is the main problem, our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the other options, including when a painkiller makes sense.

## The P6 Acupressure Point for Hangover Nausea

If nausea is your worst symptom, the one massage-style technique with real research behind it, at least in other settings, is acupressure on a point on your inner wrist called P6 (also known as PC6 or Neiguan).

**How to find it:** Turn your hand palm-up. Place the first three fingers of your other hand across your wrist, with the edge of your ring finger at the wrist crease. The P6 point sits just below your index finger, in the middle of the wrist between the two tendons you can feel there.

**How to use it:** Press firmly with your thumb for two to three minutes, using small circles or steady pressure. Repeat on the other wrist. Some people use elastic wristbands with a plastic stud that presses on the point; these are sold for motion sickness and morning sickness.

**What the evidence says:** A Cochrane systematic review on stimulating the P6 point found that it reduced nausea and vomiting after surgery compared with sham treatment, although the quality of the evidence was mixed. P6 acupressure has also been studied for motion sickness and pregnancy nausea with mixed results. There is no good evidence specifically on hangover nausea, so it's a low-cost, low-risk thing to try rather than a reliable fix. If it helps you, great. If not, you've lost nothing but a few minutes.

For the full range of options for an upset stomach, including what to eat and drink, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## Massage Guns and Foam Rollers on a Hangover

Percussion massage guns are popular, and many people reach for one when they wake up sore. They're fine for large muscles like the thighs, calves, and the meaty parts of the upper back, at a low setting. A few cautions:

- **Avoid the front and sides of your neck.** There are important blood vessels and nerves there. Keep a massage gun on muscle, not near your throat.
- **Avoid using it on your head.** A pounding device on the skull is not what a hangover headache needs.
- **Keep it light.** Dehydrated, achy muscles don't need high-intensity percussion.

Foam rolling works on the same principle as self-massage and can feel good on stiff legs and back. Go slowly and stay on the floor so you're not at risk if you get lightheaded.

## Should You Get a Massage After Drinking (the Same Night)?

This comes up on holidays, at resorts, and on bachelor and bachelorette weekends: a spa appointment booked for the evening after a long lunch with cocktails. The short answer is that it's better not to combine the two.

Alcohol widens your blood vessels, impairs your ability to judge pressure and pain, and makes nausea, dizziness, and falls more likely. A relaxed massage can deepen those effects. Many spas and therapists have a policy against treating clients who've been drinking. If you have a massage booked, keep drinking light beforehand, or move the appointment to the next morning once you've rehydrated. If you're planning a group trip with a spa day, schedule the treatments for the morning, before anyone starts drinking.

The same applies the other way: it's best not to start drinking right after a massage, especially a long or intense one. You'll likely be a bit dehydrated and very relaxed, and alcohol may hit harder than you expect.

## Massage Compared With Other Hangover Comfort Measures

Here's a rough comparison to help you decide where massage fits on a hangover day.

| Option | What it helps | What it doesn't do | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water and electrolytes | Dehydration, headache, fatigue | Doesn't fix poor sleep or stomach irritation | Low |
| Food (bland carbs, eggs, toast) | Low blood sugar, shakiness, nausea for some | Doesn't speed alcohol clearance | Low |
| Sleep or a nap | Tiredness, low mood, general recovery | Takes time | Free |
| Self-massage | Neck tension, tension headache, stress | Doesn't help dehydration or nausea much | Free |
| P6 wrist acupressure | Possibly nausea (evidence is from other settings) | Unproven for hangovers | Free |
| Professional massage | Muscle tension, aches, relaxation | Doesn't shorten the hangover | Moderate to high |
| Over-the-counter painkiller | Headache, body aches | Each has risks with alcohol | Low |
| Light walk or stretching | Stiffness, mood | Can worsen dizziness if overdone | Free |

The best mornings usually combine several of these: water and an electrolyte drink, something to eat, a pain reliever if appropriate, a nap, and then a gentle massage or a slow walk once you feel steady. Our guides on whether [sleep helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-sleep-help-a-hangover) and whether [exercise helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover) cover those options in more depth.

A note on painkillers before a massage: if you take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin for your headache, take it with food, and remember these can irritate a stomach already upset by alcohol. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver, which is already busy after drinking. Our articles on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explain the trade-offs.

## A Simple Hangover Morning Plan That Includes Massage

If you want a practical plan, this order tends to work well:

1. **On waking:** Drink a large glass of water or an electrolyte drink. Sip slowly if you're queasy.
2. **Eat something plain:** Toast, crackers, a banana, eggs, or rice. Food helps steady blood sugar and settles some stomachs.
3. **Pain relief if needed:** One standard dose of a suitable painkiller, with food, following the label.
4. **Rest:** Go back to bed for an hour or two if you can.
5. **Self-massage:** Temples, base of the skull, scalp, and shoulders, five to ten minutes. Try P6 wrist pressure if nausea is lingering.
6. **Professional massage (optional):** Once you feel steady, can keep fluids down, and are sure you're sober, book a gentle 30 to 60 minute relaxation or head-and-neck massage.
7. **Afterward:** Get up slowly, drink more water, and take it easy for the rest of the day.

Most hangovers ease within about a day. If yours seem to be lasting longer or getting worse with age, our article on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains what's typical.

## When to See a Doctor Instead of Booking a Massage

Most hangovers are unpleasant but harmless and pass on their own. Some symptoms, though, are signals that something more is going on, and a massage is the wrong response. Get medical help if:

- **You can't keep fluids down** for more than a few hours, or you keep vomiting.
- **You vomit blood** or material that looks like coffee grounds, or your stool is black.
- **You have a sudden, severe headache**, especially one that comes on like a thunderclap, or a headache with a stiff neck, fever, weakness, or trouble speaking.
- **Your muscles are severely painful, swollen, or weak**, and your urine is dark brown or you're peeing much less than usual. This can be a sign of muscle breakdown, which needs prompt care.
- **You faint**, or feel close to fainting every time you stand.
- **You have chest pain**, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, or trouble breathing.
- **You feel worse as the day goes on**, with shaking, sweating, agitation, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there. These can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous and needs medical attention, so contact a doctor or urgent care right away.
- **Someone was very drunk last night** and was confused, hard to wake, breathing slowly, or vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning; call 911.

If you notice that you need a massage, painkillers, and a full day in bed after most nights out, it's worth looking at how much and how fast you're drinking. Small changes, like alternating drinks with water and setting a limit before you go out, often make the biggest difference.

## Preventing the Aches in the First Place

The most reliable way to need less hangover recovery is to drink in a way that produces a smaller hangover. That means eating a proper meal before you drink, pacing yourself (one drink an hour or slower), alternating alcoholic drinks with water, choosing clearer drinks over darker ones if congeners bother you, and stopping a couple of hours before bed so you sleep better. Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each step.

Some people also use supplements. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, is the one we cover most on this site. Early research, mostly in animals with limited human data, suggests it may influence how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde. It's promising but not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone or that it makes heavy drinking safe. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. A supplement doesn't replace water, food, sleep, and drinking less, and it won't give you the neck relief a good massage can.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does massage help a hangover?**

Massage can ease some hangover symptoms, mainly neck and shoulder tension, tension-type headaches, muscle aches, and stress. It doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, replace lost fluids, or settle an upset stomach, and there is no good evidence that it shortens a hangover overall. Think of it as a comfort measure alongside water, food, and rest.

**Can you get a massage while hungover?**

Usually yes, as long as you're sober, have had some water and food, and aren't actively vomiting. Tell your therapist you're feeling rough, ask for lighter pressure, and start on your back or side if lying face-down makes you queasy. If you might still have alcohol in your system after a very heavy night, wait; many therapists won't treat clients who seem intoxicated.

**Does massage flush alcohol or toxins out of your body?**

No. Alcohol is processed mostly by your liver at a fairly steady rate, and massage doesn't speed that up. The idea that massage releases toxins from muscles is popular but isn't supported by evidence. Drinking water after a massage is still a good idea on a hangover day, simply because you're likely dehydrated.

**What type of massage is best for a hangover?**

A gentle Swedish or relaxation massage, or a shorter head, neck, and shoulder session, suits most people. Skip deep tissue and hot stone massage, which can leave you sorer, hotter, and dizzier when you're dehydrated. A foot massage is a good option if you'd rather sit upright.

**Is there a pressure point for hangover nausea?**

The P6 point on the inner wrist, about three finger-widths below the wrist crease between the two tendons, is the best-studied acupressure point for nausea. A Cochrane review found that stimulating it reduced nausea after surgery, but there's no good evidence specifically for hangovers. It's free and low-risk to try for two to three minutes on each wrist.

**Can a head massage help a hangover headache?**

It may help if your headache has a tension component, the tight band across your forehead or ache at the base of your skull. Gentle circles at the temples, pressure at the base of the skull, and scalp kneading are easy to do yourself. If your headache is sudden and severe, or comes with a stiff neck, fever, or weakness, see a doctor instead.

**Is it safe to get a massage after drinking alcohol the same day?**

It's better not to. Alcohol widens blood vessels and dulls your sense of pressure and pain, which makes dizziness, nausea, and over-firm pressure more likely. Many spas have policies against treating clients who've been drinking. Keep drinking light before an appointment, or move it to the next day.

**Should I drink water after a massage when hungover?**

Yes. Not because the massage released toxins, but because alcohol makes you lose more fluid than you take in, and lying in a warm room for an hour adds to that. A glass or two of water or an electrolyte drink afterward, and getting up slowly from the table, lower the chance of feeling lightheaded.
